title: CAA Chief Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act Against AI Deepfakes
excerpt: In a New York Times essay, the head of one of Hollywood's biggest talent agencies argues that the right to refuse an AI replica of your face or voice should be federal law — and that the stalled Senate bill can still pass this year.
body:
• Bryan Lourd, chief executive of talent agency CAA, used a New York Times opinion essay on Saturday to urge Congress to pass the NO FAKES Act before the year is out.
  • The bill would create a federal right to control digital replicas of your voice and likeness — built on "control, consent and compensation" — replacing a patchwork of state laws.
  • The Senate version, introduced by Sen. Chris Coons in May, cleared the Judiciary Committee in June but has not been taken up by the full Senate.
  • For readers: nothing is law yet. If the bill passes, anyone — not just celebrities — could refuse an AI replica of themselves and sue over unauthorized commercial uses.

One of Hollywood's most powerful executives has taken the fight against AI deepfakes to Congress in print. Bryan Lourd, the chief executive of Creative Artists Agency (CAA), published an opinion essay in The New York Times on Saturday urging lawmakers to pass the NO FAKES Act, the bipartisan bill that would establish federal protections against unauthorized digital replicas of a person's voice or likeness, Variety reported.

"Every one of us should have the right to say no to an unwelcome use of our likeness," Lourd wrote, in the line Variety took for its headline. He framed his intervention as a practitioner's rather than a policymaker's: "I run a global talent agency. Part of our job is to help our clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies. We regularly negotiate those deals, and I can tell you that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans."

Control, consent and compensation

The bill's framework, as both Variety and TheWrap described it, rests on three principles: control, consent and compensation. Individuals would hold the right to authorize or reject the use of their digital likeness, and companies wanting to use an authorized replica commercially would have to negotiate and pay for it. Lourd argued that Congress does not need an entirely new legal framework — the existing principles of copyright, contracts and licensing can be extended to AI replicas if federal lawmakers set one consistent standard in place of what Variety called "outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind."

His examples were not hypothetical. Lourd pointed to a dental advertisement built around a younger, AI-generated version of Tom Hanks — the actor warned his followers about it in 2023 — a content creator whose likeness was used in an advertisement for erectile dysfunction supplements, and voice actors who discovered that recordings made for research had been turned into commercial voice clones, TheWrap reported.

"What's missing is a bright-line rule affirming that right in the AI age, and it is one Congress can supply before the year is out."

— Bryan Lourd, chief executive, CAA

Where the bill stands

The NO FAKES Act was introduced in the Senate by Sen. Chris Coons in May, following an earlier attempt last year, and advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June with a bipartisan group of co-sponsors, Variety reported. The full Senate has not taken it up. Lourd's deadline — "before the year is out" — is therefore a direct pressure point: the essay is aimed at a bill that has cleared committee and stalled.

The coalition behind it is unusually broad. Variety listed supporters including SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America, the Recording Academy, the National Association of Broadcasters, the AFL-CIO, OpenAI, YouTube and IBM; TheWrap also named Google. CAA itself has worked with the Human Consent Foundation, backed by Cate Blanchett, which helps people control permissions for their likenesses when scraped by AI models, and joined an amicus brief in the New York Times' lawsuit against OpenAI noting the active licensing market for likenesses, Variety reported.

Lourd was careful to separate consent from opposition to the technology itself. "Hollywood is not afraid of new technology," he wrote, according to TheWrap, noting that artists are already signing voluntary licensing deals with AI companies. The distinction matters for readers well beyond Hollywood: the same replica technology used on film stars is used in scam calls and impersonation fraud aimed at ordinary families. A federal consent right, if the Senate acts, would give any person — not only a CAA client — a legal basis to say no.
